transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-01-16
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Asha Patel (Pyxis CTO), Liam O'Connor (Pyxis ML Eng), Sofia Reyes (Pyxis SRE)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Pyxis Cartography is evaluating Redwood for an inference platform to power geospatial mapping QA and a user-facing query assistant. Key concerns: context length (8k+ tokens), multilingual (EN/ES/FR), tool-calling to hit external tile servers and vector DB, security (VPC, KMS, SOC2), latency vs cost tradeoffs, rolling from hosted proof-of-concept to private deployment for regulated datasets. Redwood AE + SE discussed hosted, dedicated, and private options; recommended initial hosted pilot with dedicated reserved capacity for high-throughput routes; offered benchmark workshop.

Topics covered:
- model selection (open LLMs vs tuned variants)
- context/window: 8k to 32k tokens for vector+tile+prompt
- multilingual quality and hallucination risk
- tool-calling to internal APIs (tile server, vector DB, routing)
- deployment: hosted API for POC, dedicated for predictable throughput, private (VPC) for sensitive imagery data
- security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs

Transcript: (timestamps approximate, 30-45s cadence)
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making time. I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Diego, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Asha Patel: Pretty good, Maya. Thanks. We are excited. We did a quick pre-read of the deck. Just to set context, Pyxis builds cartographic products for insurance and urban planning, we have PII-ish telemetry tied to map tiles, and we need to make sure we don't leak addresses.
[00:23] Diego Ruiz: Cool, that helps. For the call today we want to understand your workloads, what you mean by "context" (like full tile histories, vector embeddings, etc.), and any constraints around latency, cost, and security.
[00:34] Liam O'Connor: Our primary user flow is a map QA assistant — user uploads a new tile, we run a QA prompt that stitches last 10k tokens of vector context plus recent telemetry, then we call a tool that runs a geospatial check. Target latency for the assistant is about 600–800ms tail for the experience, and throughput is around 60 qps during peak.
[00:52] Sofia Reyes: On the infra side we prefer VPC peering for the private deployment but for the POC we can accept hosted with strict egress controls. KMS integration is required for keys.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Good, that's very concrete. Diego — thoughts on model family?
[01:09] Diego Ruiz: Given the long context and domain specificity, we typically evaluate two axes: architecture/size for quality and quantization/latency for cost. For 8k–32k contexts we usually recommend a family of open models that support longer context windows — some LlamaX variants and the new Longformer-style variants we validated. For customers that need best-in-class hallucination reduction on geospatial prompts, we'll consider a tuned model or an instruction-tuned 13B+ that worked well in our benchmarks.
[01:33] Asha Patel: When you say "worked well" can you quantify? We ran an in-house eval vs OpenAI earlier and saw better factuality with some of Anthropic's models, cost was higher though.
[01:44] Diego Ruiz: Right. In our tests, a tuned 13B open model delivered comparable factuality to the Anthropic baseline on geospatial QAs when given local context (vector embeddings + tile metadata). It cost about ~40% less on token compute when run with 4-bit quantization and continuous KV caching enabled. That said, Anthropic still had edge cases for hallucinations.
[02:05] Liam O'Connor: Continuous KV caching — is that the prefix cache we talked about in the docs? How does that affect memory footprint across requests?
[02:13] Diego Ruiz: Yeah that's the one. The runtime keeps hot KV state for recently used prefixes to avoid recomputing the key/value and reduce token compute. It reduces p99 latencies for repeated prefixes, but if your prefixes are very unique per request (e.g., big different tile histories) the benefit is smaller. Memory overhead is configurable per model pool; we'll size it with you.
[02:33] Sofia Reyes: For our case prefixes will be similar for tiles in the same region — we should see gains. Another question: tool-calling. We need the model to call our internal tile validation API and a vector DB to fetch nearest neighbors. Does Redwood support that flow?
[02:46] Maya Chen: Yes, we support function/tool calling and can do structured outputs. For hosted customers we provide safe-call routing and can integrate with webhooks or private connectors through VPC for dedicated/private setups. Diego can explain limitations.
[02:58] Diego Ruiz: Implementationally, we can route tool calls via a secure connector. In private deployments the connector runs inside your VPC and the model can call internal endpoints directly. For hosted we typically proxy calls through a secured tunnel and apply allow-lists and auditing. Note: long-running synchronous calls can affect surface latency — we often recommend async invocations with a small queue for heavier validations.
[03:24] Asha Patel: That makes sense. For POC we'd probably do hosted with proxying. For production we want private with VPC connectors.
[03:31] Maya Chen: Totally reasonable. On the model side, do you have language needs beyond English?
[03:36] Liam O'Connor: Yes, English + Spanish and occasional French. Not heavy for FR but we need strong EN/ES parity. Also domain-specific terms like cadastral and parcel IDs, which get garbled a lot.
[03:49] Diego Ruiz: We include language-specific evals in our onboarding and can recommend models with good multilingual performance. Some open models are stronger in ES than others; we sometimes run small instruction-tuning passes with domain lexicons to raise ES precision.
[04:04] Asha Patel: Is that tuning something Redwood does or we do?
[04:07] Diego Ruiz: We can support both. For enterprise customers we have an options page — Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and tuning. For sensitive data, you can run the tuning job in your private deployment or we can run it on dedicated capacity under a contract with data handling guarantees.
[04:22] Maya Chen: On security, SSO and audit logs are must-haves per Asha's note. We have SOC2, support SAML/SCIM, RBAC, and detailed per-token audit logs. We'll send the SOC2 package.
[04:34] Sofia Reyes: How granular are the audit logs? We need to map tokens back to tenant IDs and store an immutable trail for compliance.
[04:41] Diego Ruiz: We can include token-level metadata and route logs to your SIEM. For private deployments you control the log retention and storage. In hosted we have configurable retention windows and can ship to your S3 or Splunk via secure forwarding.
[04:56] Liam O'Connor: Performance — you mentioned 60 qps with 600–800ms tail. What's the expected cost if we run that 8 hours a day with the tuned 13B?
[05:06] Maya Chen: I'll share the pricing spreadsheet but ballpark: with dedicated reserved pools you can get predictable per-token costs and often 30–50% savings vs bursty hosted usage. For sustained 60 qps on a tuned 13B, dedicated nodes with optimized kernels and 4-bit quantization is usually most cost effective. We'll model exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
[05:26] Asha Patel: For the POC we want a quick baseline — maybe 2 weeks, validate accuracy and tools. Then scale to dedicated for production. Is that a typical path?
[05:33] Diego Ruiz: That's exactly what we recommend. Start hosted POC (2–3 weeks), measure p50/p95/p99 and quality versus your eval set. If throughput and latency are acceptable move to dedicated reserved capacity. If data residency/regulatory constraints exist, we pivot to private VPC deployment.
[05:50] Sofia Reyes: Any gotchas with on-prem? We do have some regulated imagery that can't leave our network.
[05:55] Diego Ruiz: On-prem packages require additional lead time for network/IP allow-lists, HSM/KMS integration, and we do an install window. Also some specialized kernels for older GPUs might not be available — we can share a compatibility matrix.
[06:10] Asha Patel: Competitors: we did talk to OpenAI and Anthropic — they have strong base models, but integration and cost for long contexts was a blocker. How does Redwood compare?
[06:19] Maya Chen: Redwood is model-agnostic and focuses on serving: we give you predictable latency/cost levers and a single API across hosted/dedicated/private. We'll show benchmark comparisons but the key is operational controls: batching, KV caching, routing policies, and fallback models.
[06:36] Liam O'Connor: About rollouts — we need canarying and automatic fallback if latency spikes. Support for A/B and gradual rollout?
[06:44] Diego Ruiz: Yes, the Redwood Console supports canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to cheaper or lower-latency model variants. You can pin models per route and set policy by latency or cost thresholds.
[06:55] Asha Patel: Ok, sounds good. A couple of nitty gritty: data redaction, PII scrubbing before logs, and rate-limiting per tenant.
[07:04] Maya Chen: We have built-in redaction hooks — you can configure pre-ingest scrubbing or post-response masking. Tenant-level quotas and rate-limits are supported.
[07:13] Sofia Reyes: Great. For the benchmark plan, we will provide 500 sample prompts and a week of telemetry. What format do you need?
[07:21] Diego Ruiz: CSV for prompts with metadata columns (language, tile_id, timestamp) and a tarball for a small subset of tiles. We'll send a data schema and secure upload instructions.
[07:32] Asha Patel: Onboarding timeline — if everything goes well, we want POC this month and production next quarter. Is that feasible?
[07:40] Maya Chen: Yes, with a fast POC in hosted we can typically hit production timeline in 8–12 weeks if you need dedicated or private fewer for added lead time for private.
[07:51] Liam O'Connor: Any blockers for getting started? Contracts, IP, or data processing agreements?
[07:56] Maya Chen: We'll send a standard MSA and DPA; for private deployments we add an install schedule and acceptance criteria. Procurement questions often pop up but we've run similar deals.
[08:07] Asha Patel: Sounds like next steps are clear: pricing + SOC2 + network diagram, benchmark plan, and sample data.
[08:13] Maya Chen: Yup. Diego, anything else to add?
[08:16] Diego Ruiz: I'll include a recommended model shortlist: 13B tuned open model (long context), a 30k-context variant we validated for long transcripts, and a smaller 7B variant for low-cost routes. Also a note on quantization tradeoffs.
[08:32] Sofia Reyes: Can you call out any known limitations of the long-context models? We saw tokenization artifacts with long IDs and some hallucination when embedding context from disparate vector chunks.
[08:43] Diego Ruiz: Sure — long contexts can exacerbate hallucination if the context isn't well filtered. We recommend chunking heuristics, provenance markers, and small pre-prompts to bias the model. We'll include examples in the benchmark plan.
[08:58] Maya Chen: Great. Quick recap and owners of next steps: Maya to send pricing, SOC2, network diagram; Diego to send benchmark plan + model shortlist; Asha/Liam to provide sample data and target SLAs. Any other items?
[09:12] Asha Patel: No, that's it. Thanks both.
[09:16] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up by email and set the technical workshop.
[09:20] (end)

Notes (imperfect auto-transcription): occasional speaker labels merged, some product names transcribed as "Longformer style" or "LlamaX" etc, "KV cash" appears once instead of "KV cache". References to pricing and SOC2 are placeholders — see attachments.
